title: Tile Bench
context: Grade 4, the recap. An adult sees tiles being laid. What is actually being settled is what the test for a tessellation is. The page's first sentence says without any gaps or overlaps, its definition then drops the overlaps, and nothing on the page says what a gap is, so a child who reads the test literally can reject a correct tiling because its outline is bumpy. The gap finder draws that line for the child: a gap is a space with tiles closed round it, and the uneven outer edge is only where the tiling stops.

writeup.why: Lay copies of one shape side by side, test the patch for gaps and for overlaps, carry a tiling on, and make a pattern out of everyday things.
writeup.look: A bench of dotted paper with a tray of shapes along its top edge, a gap finder and an overlap finder, and an object tray at one side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Tile Bench' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the copies laid against the copies this phase asks for, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each copy or each thing is set down, and the second is fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The shape tray runs along the top edge of the working area, 1086 by 90 at 64,206. It holds squares, rectangles, triangles, hexagons, circles and a few shapes made of joined squares, all at matching sizes. A tile drawn taller than it is wide is a rectangle and is never called a square. The bench of dotted paper lies under the tray, 760 by 320 at 64,306, with grey dots every 40 in both directions. Copies are dragged down from the tray, turned with the turn control before they are set down, and snap to the dots. The gap finder washes over the patch when it is tapped. It fills every space that has tiles closed round it on every side, solid reddish purple. It traces the uneven outline round the outside of the patch in a plain near-black line and leaves it unfilled, because that is where the tiling stops. The overlap finder shades any part where two copies lie on top of each other, in reddish purple hatching. A doubled part and a gap are told apart by their marks as well as by the finder that found them. A patch is named a tessellation only when both finders come back empty. Carry on offers a near-black dashed outline of the next copy where the tiling would repeat it, which the child sets down or moves. The object tray stands at the right, 310 by 320 at 840,306, holding marigolds, roses, leaves, coins, bottle caps and buttons. Things are laid along a string or in rows on the bench, and the bracket lights every copy of a chosen group. The can do list runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 72 at 64,648, carrying the chapter's four statements with a tick box beside each. A statement can be ticked only against work standing on the bench. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is two verdict keys, tessellation and not a tessellation, over two keys for a space, gap and edge. Twelve number keys three across take over wherever a count is asked for. On the fourth phase the pad holds the four word cards, number pattern, series, secret code and tessellation, each turning over to a meaning. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A circle is never squeezed or flattened to close a gap, and two tiles are never drawn overlapping unless the frame is showing an overlap on purpose. The bench draws shapes as they are, so what the finders report is about the shapes and never about the drawing.
writeup.finish: The card shows the patch the child tiled with both finders empty, the pattern of things they laid out with its repeating group bracketed, and the can do list as they ticked it.

phases.win: both finders come back empty and the patch is named a tessellation
phases.does: lays copies of one shape side by side, then runs the gap finder and the overlap finder
phases.goal: copies of one shape set side by side with no gaps and no overlaps make a tessellation
phases.says: Lay the copies side by side. Is anything left uncovered? Is anything doubled?
phases.check: Away from the screen: lay coins touching on a table. Is anything left uncovered? Is anything doubled?
phases.feels: a patch passes only when nothing is left uncovered and nothing lies on top of anything else
phases.hands: Cut squares, triangles, hexagons and circles to matching sizes, and give each group one kind of shape to cover a sheet of paper with. Keep both halves of the test from the first sentence the page prints: no gaps and no overlaps. Lay one square half over another and ask whether that counts. Then ask which groups managed it, which were left with spaces, and why the circles could not.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: is any space left between the copies? Second rung, the phase's: does any copy lie over another? Third rung: the patch is cut to two copies side by side, and the child runs both finders on them. The verdict keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the page's definition and its summary box speak only of gaps, and a patch with nothing uncovered seems to pass that test.
wrong.move: lays copies overlapping to cover every bit of the bench, and names the patch a tessellation because nothing is left uncovered.
wrong.screen: the overlap finder shades every doubled part in reddish purple hatching, while the gap finder comes back empty. The patch is not named, and the child's tiles stay exactly where they were laid. The voice asks whether anything is doubled.

wrong.why: a space that shrinks each time the circles are pushed closer seems as though it must close if they are pushed hard enough.
wrong.move: pushes the circles harder together to close the spaces between them, and calls the gaps gone once every circle touches its neighbours.
wrong.screen: the gap finder fills the curved spaces between the circles, and they stay however the circles are pushed. A circle pushed further lands over its neighbour, and the overlap finder shades that part. No circle is ever squeezed out of shape to close a space.

phases.screen: an empty bench with the shape tray loaded and both finders waiting
phases.soWhat: Copies of one shape set side by side with no gaps and no overlaps make a tessellation.
phases.concept: Copies that fit with no gaps

phases.win: a closed-in space fills while the outer edge is traced plain and left empty
phases.does: runs the gap finder and decides whether each space it shows is a gap or only the edge
phases.goal: a gap is a space with tiles closed round it, and the bumpy outer edge is not a gap
phases.says: Is this space closed in by tiles all round? Or is it where the tiling stops?
phases.check: Away from the screen: lay six tiles in a patch. Point to its edge, and say whether the patch has any gap.
phases.feels: a gap is shut in by tiles all round, and the bumpy outside edge is only where the tiles stop
phases.hands: Lay a patch of paper hexagons on a desk and ask whether the bumps round its outline are gaps. Run a finger round each space: a gap is a space with tiles closed round it on every side. Settle that the outline is only where the tiling stops. Then lay octagons in rows, and ask about the small square spaces closed in between them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is this space closed in by tiles on every side? Second rung, the phase's: can a finger run from it to the outside without crossing a tile? Third rung: the patch is cut to three tiles round one space, and the child traces it. The verdict keys and the space keys stay open.

wrong.why: the page tests for gaps and never says what a gap is, and a notch is a space the eye can see.
wrong.move: calls the notches round the outer edge gaps, and rejects a patch that fits perfectly inside.
wrong.screen: the gap finder washes over the patch and fills nothing, and the outer edge is traced in its plain line and left empty. A tracer is run into one notch and straight out again to the outside. The child's verdict stays in the slot, and the patch is named.

wrong.why: the edge has just been set aside as not a gap, and a space near it seems to belong to it.
wrong.move: calls a space closed in near the outline only the edge, because it sits close to where the tiling stops.
wrong.screen: the gap finder fills that space solid, because tiles close round it on every side. The tracer runs round inside it and never reaches the outside. The child's answer stays beside the patch.

phases.screen: a patch of tiles with a bumpy outline and, in some patches, a space closed in the middle
phases.soWhat: A gap is a space with tiles closed round it on every side, and the uneven outer edge of a patch is not a gap.
phases.concept: A gap or only the edge

phases.win: each new copy snaps into place against the last and both finders stay empty
phases.does: sets down the next copies one at a time where the tiling repeats
phases.goal: a tiling is carried on by repeating the same shape the same way, with no gap and no overlap
phases.says: Where does the next one go? Which way must it face?
phases.check: A row of triangles starts point up, and they take turns. Which way does the seventh point?
phases.feels: each copy fits against the last one in the same way, so the tiling can go on across the bench
phases.hands: On dotted paper, draw two copies of a shape made of joined squares side by side, and ask where the third goes. Count the dots from the start of one copy to the start of the next. Draw five more the same way, each starting the same number of dots after the last. Then do the same with a row of triangles, and ask which way each new one must point.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which way does the last copy face? Second rung, the phase's: where does the next copy touch the last? Third rung: the row is cut to two copies and one dashed outline, and the child sets one copy down. The verdict keys stay open.

wrong.why: the first triangle pointed up, and copying the first one looks like repeating the shape.
wrong.move: sets every new triangle point up, leaving a space between each pair.
wrong.screen: the gap finder fills the triangular space between each pair in reddish purple. Carry on then offers the next copy as a dashed outline turned point down, fitted against the last. The child's triangles stay where they were set.

wrong.why: copies of one shape look alike wherever they sit, and one dot is a small distance to see.
wrong.move: starts the next copy one dot too far along, leaving a thin space, or one dot too near, so it lies over the last.
wrong.screen: both finders run, and a thin space fills with the wash or a doubled strip is hatched. Carry on's dashed outline stands where the tiling repeats, and the child's copy stays beside it. The dots between the starts of two copies are counted aloud.

phases.screen: two or three copies of a shape laid on the dotted paper, with room for more to the right
phases.soWhat: A tiling is carried on by repeating the same shape the same way, with no gap and no overlap.

phases.win: the bracket lights every copy of the group along the string
phases.does: lays out things in a pattern, then brackets the group that repeats
phases.goal: everyday things make a pattern when a group of them repeats
phases.says: Make a pattern of your own. Which group comes round again?
phases.check: Away from the screen: make a pattern with pencils, erasers and caps. Ask a friend to find the group.
phases.feels: any things at all make a pattern, once a group of them comes round again
phases.hands: Let groups make a toran of paper marigolds, roses and leaves on a string, each group choosing its own group to repeat. Swap torans and have the others find the group that repeats and say it aloud. Then set bottle caps in rows whose colours swap like a chessboard, and ask what the next row starts with. The can do list's last statement says the child can make tessellation patterns, and no printed exercise asks for one. So let every child make one on the bench and tick the statement against it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which group comes round again? Second rung, the phase's: how many things are in one group? Third rung: the string is cut to two copies of the group, and the child brackets one. The number keys and the word cards stay open.

wrong.why: marigolds and roses are both flowers, and the question asks about one kind of flower among several.
wrong.move: counts every flower as a marigold, writing six for a string of marigold, leaf, leaf, rose repeated three times.
wrong.screen: the bracket over the group of four lights every copy along the string, and the marigold of each copy is lit on its own. The roses stay unlit. The child's six stays in the slot beside the three lit marigolds.

wrong.why: the second row ended on red, and the colour after red along a row has always been cream.
wrong.move: starts the third row of caps with cream, carrying the second row straight on from its last cap.
wrong.screen: the rows are bracketed one under another, and the colour at the start of each row is lit down the left edge: red, cream, and the one still to come. The child's third row stays drawn under the bench's own.

phases.screen: the object tray open beside an empty string and two empty rows
phases.soWhat: Everyday things make a pattern when a group of them repeats.
phases.concept: Patterns made from things around you

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the gap finder is tapped. A wash pours down over the patch from the top of the bench like water. It runs off every notch and bump of the outline and away off the bench, and settles only in the spaces with tiles closed round them. Those fill slowly from the bottom up, and the outline is left traced in its plain line with nothing in its notches. It pours as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the bench stands empty with the shape tray loaded and both finders waiting. On the second a patch of tiles stands with a bumpy outline, and in some patches a space closed in somewhere inside. On the third two or three copies of a shape lie on the dotted paper with room for more to their right. On the fourth the object tray is open beside an empty string and two empty rows, with the can do list along the foot. The running count at the top left holds the copies laid against the copies this phase asks for, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once, the first shape in the tray or the gap finder or the last copy laid or the first thing in the object tray. It gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what goes next. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any shape from the tray on the bench, and any things from the object tray, with both finders and the carry on control open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on gaps and overlaps, a gap against the edge, carrying a tiling on, and patterns and words from the whole chapter.
voiceLines: A bench of dotted paper and a tray of shapes. Lay the first copy down.
Lay the copies side by side. Is anything left uncovered? Is anything doubled?
Is this space closed in by tiles all round? Or is it where the tiling stops?
Where does the next one go? Which way must it face?
Make a pattern of your own. Which group comes round again?
Another patch. Look for spaces inside it, and for tiles lying on top.
Free play. Any shape, any things from the tray, with both finders open.
Run both finders again, and look at what each one shows.
Every patch tested for gaps and for overlaps, and a pattern of your own laid out.

observations.why: The test has two halves, and covering everything answers only one of them.
observations.soWhat: A tessellation needs no gaps and no overlaps, both at once.
observations.observe: The patch of overlapping squares covered everything, and still the overlap finder shaded it.

observations.why: A gap has tiles closed round it on every side, while the outline is open to the outside.
observations.soWhat: The uneven outer edge of a patch is not a gap; it is only where the tiling stops.
observations.observe: The wash filled the space closed in between four circles, and ran off the bumpy outline of the hexagons.

observations.why: The same shape turned the same way repeats the same fit, copy after copy.
observations.soWhat: A tiling is carried on by repeating the same shape the same way.
observations.observe: Each copy the carry on control offered touched the last one exactly, and both finders stayed empty.

observations.why: Things make a pattern when a group of them comes round again, whatever the things are.
observations.soWhat: Everyday things make a pattern when a group of them repeats.
observations.observe: The bracket lit every copy of the group along the string of flowers and leaves.

source_tool.name: Tile Bench
source_tool.blurb: Lay copies of one shape side by side, test for gaps and for overlaps, carry a tiling on, and make a pattern from everyday things.

serves.exercise: identifying which of the three figures are tessellations
adding five more unit shapes to each of the two tilings on dotted paper

source_tool.description: A bench of dotted paper fills the stage with a tray of shapes along its top edge: squares, rectangles, triangles, hexagons, circles, and a few shapes made of joined squares. Copies are dragged down onto the bench and snap to the dots, and each copy can be turned before it is set down. A gap finder washes over the patch when it is tapped and fills every space that has tiles closed round it on every side, while the uneven outline round the outside of the patch is traced in a plain line and left unfilled, so a space inside the patch and the edge where the tiling stops are never confused. An overlap finder shades any place where two copies lie on top of each other. A patch is named a tessellation only when both finders come back empty. A carry on control takes the last copy laid and offers the next one where the tiling would repeat it, which the child sets down or moves, so a tiling is extended a copy at a time. An object tray holds flowers, leaves, coins, bottle caps and buttons, which can be laid along a string or in rows to make a pattern of things, with a bracket to mark the group that repeats. A can do list along the foot of the stage carries the chapter's four statements to tick against work standing on the bench, and a set of word cards holds its four words.
source_tool.art_direction: A bench of dotted paper and tiles / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip of picture cells, a paper arrow on a dial, stepping stones with jump arcs between them, counters that pair up, a tower of boxes each resting on two below, two rings of letters that turn, a ruled board of sums with a slate beside it, and a bench of dotted paper with a tray of tiles.
A repeating group is always shown whole. When a bracket is drawn over it, every copy of it along the row is lit at once, and a copy that does not match is left unlit rather than hidden.

Every step in a series is drawn as an arc from one term to the next with its label on the arc, never as a bare number between two terms, so the step between every pair of neighbours can be read, not only the first.
A counting-down track has a zero stone at its left end and nothing beyond it. No track, board or list is ever drawn running on past zero.

Every box of a number tower rests visibly on exactly two boxes below it, and the operation sign is drawn between each pair of neighbours in every row, so a tower that keeps to one operation shows the same sign all the way up.
The alphabet is always drawn round a circle, twenty-six letters evenly spaced, so the last letter sits beside the first and no letter ever falls off an end.
A line put back into a board is drawn sliding into its place between its neighbours, and the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand, never cleared.

Tiles are drawn at true relative size, edge to edge where they touch, never overlapping unless the frame is showing an overlap on purpose, and a circle is never squeezed to close a gap. A tile drawn taller than it is wide is never called a square.
A shape, a term or a box is told apart by its label or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a shape, a term, a box, a letter or a tile the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Whatever the stage hands over, a printed term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter of a message and a tile already laid, is deep blue, and so is the first member of a repeating group. The second member of a repeating group, and a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself, a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, the operation sign between two boxes and the shift a key makes from a letter to its partner, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is the rule cannot afford a frame where the step has to be hunted for. Whatever the rule makes, a next term, a box built from the two below it, a coded or decoded letter, a tile carried on and a tick on the can do list, is green. Whatever the child is asked to notice, a box that breaks the tower's operation, a space with tiles closed round it, a part where two tiles lie on top of each other, a counter left without a partner and a missing line put back on a board, is reddish purple. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome, and the outer edge of a tiled patch is traced in that plain line and never filled, because it is where the tiling stops and not a gap. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box and never a faded copy of its answer. All of that holds in greyscale, because a jump label sits on its own arc, a broken box keeps its light on after the check has moved past it, a closed-in gap is filled while the outer edge is only outlined, and a leftover counter stands apart from the pairs.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Run both finders again, and look at what each one shows.
voice.onNext: Another patch. Look for spaces inside it, and for tiles lying on top.
voice.opening: A bench of dotted paper and a tray of shapes. Lay the first copy down.
voice.onFinish: Every patch tested for gaps and for overlaps, and a pattern of your own laid out.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any shape, any things from the tray, with both finders open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Copies that fit with no gaps
A gap or only the edge
Patterns made from things around you

placement.where: After groups have tried to cover a sheet of paper with cut-out squares, triangles, hexagons and circles, and before the printed figures are judged. The tool is what fills only the spaces with tiles closed round them and traces the outer edge in a plain line, which a drawing on paper leaves to the reader's eye.

answer_key.rule: Copies of one shape placed side by side with no gaps and no overlaps make a tessellation, and shapes that can do it are said to tessellate. Both conditions matter: shapes lying over one another do not make a tessellation even when nothing is left uncovered. A gap is a space with tiles closed round it on every side. The uneven outline round the outside of a tiled patch is not a gap; it is only where the tiling stops. Circles cannot tessellate, because gaps are left between them however they are pushed together. A tiling is carried on by repeating the same shape the same way, each new copy touching the last with no gap and no overlap. Everyday things make a pattern when a group of them repeats.
answer_key.wrong: Both finders are run over the patch again, the gap finder filling only spaces with tiles closed round them and the overlap finder shading only doubled parts, while the outer edge is traced in a plain line so that it is seen to be the edge. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Look for a space with bricks closed round it. There is none, so there are no gaps.
Look for a brick lying over another. There is none, so there are no overlaps.
Copies of one shape with no gaps and no overlaps make a tessellation, so the wall is one.
items.answer: Yes. The bricks fit side by side with no gaps and no overlaps, so the wall is a tessellation
items.question: Rectangular bricks are laid in rows on a wall, each row moved along by half a brick. Is any space left between them, and does any brick lie over another? Is the wall a tessellation?
items.checkpoint: A tessellation needs both: no gaps and no overlaps.
items.misconception: Checking only for gaps, and forgetting that tiles lying over one another also break a tessellation.

steps: A gap is a space with tiles closed round it on every side.
The notches along the top are open to the outside, so they are the edge of the patch and not a gap.
Inside the patch no space is left and no tile lies over another, so the patch is a tessellation.
items.answer: Yes. The notches are only where the tiling stops, so they are not a gap, and nothing inside the patch is left uncovered
items.question: A patch of triangle tiles has a zig-zag outline, with notches all along its top edge. No space is left inside the patch. Is it a tessellation?
items.checkpoint: The uneven outer edge of a patch is not a gap; it is only where the tiling stops.
items.misconception: Calling the notches round the edge gaps, and rejecting a patch that fits perfectly inside.

steps: The triangles take turns, up then down, and each shares a side with the one before it.
The last one points up, so the next points down, then up, then down.
Each new triangle fits against the last with no gap and no overlap, so the tiling carries on.
items.answer: Point down, point up, point down
items.question: A row of triangles on dotted paper goes point up, point down, point up. Three more are to be added. Which way does each one point?
items.checkpoint: A tiling is carried on by repeating the same shape the same way.
items.misconception: Setting every new triangle point up, which leaves a space between each pair.

steps: The group that repeats is marigold, leaf, leaf, rose, which is four pieces.
Twelve pieces hold three whole groups, because 3 x 4 = 12.
Each group has one marigold, so there are three marigolds.
items.answer: Three, because the group of four repeats three times in twelve pieces
items.question: A toran repeats marigold, leaf, leaf, rose along its string. The string holds twelve pieces. How many marigolds are on it?
items.checkpoint: Things make a pattern when a group of them repeats.
items.misconception: Counting every flower as a marigold, and writing six.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Round coins are laid touching one another on a table. Is this a tessellation?
items.final_answer: No. Circles leave gaps between them, however they are pushed together

items.question: Two square tiles are laid so that one lies half over the other. Nothing is left uncovered between them. Is this a tessellation?
items.final_answer: No. There are no gaps, but one tile overlaps the other, and a tessellation needs no gaps and no overlaps

items.question: A patch of diamond-shaped tiles has a saw-tooth outline down both sides. Are the teeth gaps?
items.final_answer: No. The saw-tooth outline is only where the tiling stops, so it is not a gap

items.question: Circles are packed in rows, and a small space with four curved sides is closed in between every four circles. Is that space a gap, or only the edge?
items.final_answer: A gap, because circles close round it on every side, so the circles are not a tessellation

items.question: Dominoes, each two squares long and one square high, are laid end to end in a row. Four are down. How long is the row, in squares, after three more are added?
items.final_answer: 14 squares, because seven dominoes each two squares long make 14

items.question: In a row of triangles, the first points up and they take turns, up and down. Which way does the tenth triangle point?
items.final_answer: Down. The odd-numbered triangles point up and the even-numbered ones point down, and ten is even

items.question: Blue and yellow buttons are set out in three rows of five, with the colours swapping like a chessboard. The first row starts with blue. What colour starts the third row, and how many buttons are blue?
items.final_answer: Blue starts the third row, and 8 buttons are blue: 3 in the first row, 2 in the second and 3 in the third

items.question: Name the chapter word for each of these. A floor of tiles with no gaps and no overlaps. A message that can be read only with its key. A list of numbers in order that follows a rule.
items.final_answer: A tessellation; a secret code; a series, whose rule is its number pattern

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Cut squares, triangles, hexagons and circles to matching sizes before the tool is opened, and let groups try to cover a sheet with one kind of shape. Keep both halves of the test from the first sentence the page prints: no gaps and no overlaps. The page's definition and its summary box keep the gaps and drop the overlaps, so lay one tile half over another and ask whether that counts. Then say what a gap is, because the page never does: a space with tiles closed round it on every side. Lay a patch of paper hexagons, ask whether the bumps round its outline are gaps, and settle that the outline is only where the tiling stops. Two of the three printed figures in the exercise have notched outlines, and a child reading the test literally rejects both, which are the two correct answers. The tiles in the third figure are drawn taller than they are wide; do not call them squares. The last statement of the self-assessment says the child can make tessellation patterns, and no printed exercise asks for one, so let every child make one on the bench and tick the statement against it. The four vocabulary words are number pattern, series, secret code and tessellation, and only the last is given a definition on the page; give the other three a meaning on the back of each card in the class's own words.
generation_prompt: Build a tiling tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. The working area is a bench of dotted paper, the dots evenly spaced, with a tray along its top edge holding squares, rectangles, triangles, regular hexagons, circles and a few shapes made of joined squares, all at matching sizes. Copies are dragged onto the bench and snap to the dots, and a turn control rotates a copy before it is set down. A gap finder, when tapped, fills every region that is enclosed by tiles on every side and traces the outer outline of the patch in a plain unfilled line. An overlap finder shades any region where two copies lie on top of each other. A patch is named a tessellation only when both finders come back empty. A carry on control offers a ghost of the next copy where the tiling would repeat it, which the child can set down or move. An object tray at one side holds marigolds, roses, leaves, coins, bottle caps and buttons that can be laid along a string or in rows, with a bracket control that lights every copy of a chosen group. A can do list of four statements with tick boxes runs along the foot of the working area, and four word cards turn over to show a meaning. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Lay copies of one shape side by side. Tap the gap finder. Tap the overlap finder. A bumpy outside edge is not a gap. Add the next copy the same way. Make a pattern with things from the tray.
